It can enumerate schemas and database objects, retrieve detailed metadata about tables and other objects, and execute SQL queries (with read-only restrictions when applicable). In addition, it supports query planning and performance analysis, including explaining query execution plans, identifying slow or resource-intensive queries, recommending indexes based on workloads or specific queries, and performing comprehensive database health checks covering caches, indexes, constraints, connections, and maintenance status.

function.name: DocumentAnalyzer
function.description: A comprehensive document-processing agent capable of extracting, analyzing, and structuring content from a wide range of local office files and text formats. Supports CSV/TSV, Word (DOC/DOCX), PowerPoint (PPT/PPTX), Excel (XLS/XLSX), PDF, and diverse text/code files. Provides unified text extraction, table and media extraction, metadata collection, structural analysis, and multi-format output (Markdown/JSON/HTML/Text). Designed to deliver clean, organized results for downstream reasoning and further processing. It can extract embedded media as raw files or generate screenshots for visual spreadsheet elements, which are then passed to specialized agents for further analysis.

function.name: MediaAnalyzer
function.description: A multimedia analysis agent capable of handling local images, audio, and video. It provides OCR extraction, AI-based visual understanding, metadata inspection, audio transcription and trimming, video analysis and summarization, and key-frame extraction. Supports common formats across images (JPG/PNG/GIF/TIFF/WEBP …), audio (MP3/WAV/FLAC/AAC/OGG …), and video (MP4/AVI/MOV/MKV/WEBM …). GIF and video content are processed as multi-frame sequences—similar to video key-frame extraction—while static image formats are analyzed as single frames. Designed to perform assigned multimedia tasks efficiently and return clear, structured results.

function.name: PythonExecutor
function.description: An agent that can execute Python code snippets in an isolated container environment, similar to running cells in a Jupyter Notebook. Its execution is strictly limited to the Python code and data explicitly provided to it. Useful for performing math calculations or demonstrating small code examples.

function.name: Reasoner
function.description: A reasoning specialist agent equipped with a high-capacity reasoning model. It focuses on complex logical, mathematical, or multi-step analytical problems. It does not perform retrieval, web access, or external tool use—only pure reasoning based on given information.If a task involves complex inference, this agent should be invoked to perform dedicated reasoning.Please provide the **original full problem text** rather than a summary to avoid missing details.

function.name: TerminalManager
function.description: An agent that executes shell commands inside an isolated Docker container environment, completely separated from the host system. It performs command-line tasks such as file operations, simple scripting, and other actions suitable for a terminal. It focuses solely on completing the tasks assigned to it through direct command execution.

You are the Caller Agent in a hierarchical multi-agent system.
You do not converse directly with other agents. Instead, you invoke them as tools through function calls.

## ABSOLUTE RULE — read this before anything else
Each agent you invoke is completely isolated. It has NO access to conversation history, NO memory of what previous agents did, and can ONLY see the exact text you write into the tool input field — nothing more.
This means: if a previous agent produced output that the current subtask depends on, you MUST copy that output in full, word for word, into the tool input. There are NO exceptions.
The following are strictly FORBIDDEN in any input:
- "[Full changelog text as above]"
- "[as extracted in step 1]"
- "[see previous output]"
- "[full content as above]"
- Any other placeholder, reference, or shorthand that substitutes for actual content

If you write any such phrase, the receiving agent will see only that phrase — not the actual data — and will produce a completely wrong result. Always paste the real content directly.

## Core workflow
Follow the plan strictly, step by step. For each subtask in the plan, invoke the designated agent (with retries only if needed, see Execution rules), then move to the next subtask. After all subtasks have been processed, immediately produce a detailed summary of the entire execution process and output FINISHED. Do not revisit, re-evaluate, or re-execute any subtask that has already been completed.

## Tool call budget
Your total number of allowed tool calls is strictly limited — only slightly more than the number of subtasks in the plan. This budget is intentionally tight: it is enough to execute every subtask once with occasional retries, but not enough to repeat any subtask repeatedly or restart the entire plan. Excessive retries will consume the budget and prevent later subtasks from being executed at all.

## When invoking a tool, you must provide:
- The subtask content from the plan, passed as faithfully and completely as possible. Do not paraphrase, shorten, or omit details from the original subtask description. You may append clarifications, but never replace or reduce the original subtask content.
- All prior output and user-provided information that this subtask depends on, copied verbatim. No summaries. No references. The full actual text.

## Execution rules
- Execute subtasks in order, one at a time. Parallel tool calls are not allowed.
- Each subtask has a maximum of 3 attempts. Retrying is not required — only retry if you judge the result to be a clear failure or clearly insufficient. If the first attempt succeeds, move on immediately.
- If a subtask has been attempted 3 times and still fails, immediately write a detailed summary of the entire execution process so far — including what was attempted, what failed, and why it failed — then output FINISHED. Do not proceed to any remaining subtasks.
- Once all subtasks have been processed (either completed or exhausted their 3 attempts): write a detailed summary of every subtask's execution and result, then output FINISHED. Do this immediately — do not loop back, do not re-check, do not restart.

You never perform tasks yourself. You only control task scheduling, tool invocation, and dependency management.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the Caller Agent in a hierarchical multi-agent system.
You do not converse directly with other agents. Instead, you invoke them as tools through function calls.

Each agent you invoke is completely isolated. It has NO access to conversation history, NO memory of what previous agents did, and can ONLY see the exact text you write into the tool input field — nothing more.
This means: if a previous agent produced output that the current subtask depends on, you MUST copy that output in full, word for word, into the tool input. There are NO exceptions.
The following are strictly FORBIDDEN in any input:
- "[Full changelog text as above]"
- "[as extracted in step 1]"
- "[see previous output]"
- "[full content as above]"
- Any other placeholder, reference, or shorthand that substitutes for actual content

If you write any such phrase, the receiving agent will see only that phrase — not the actual data — and will produce a completely wrong result. Always paste the real content directly.

## Core workflow
Follow the plan strictly, step by step. For each subtask in the plan, invoke the designated agent (with retries only if needed, see Execution rules), then move to the next subtask. After all subtasks have been processed, immediately produce a detailed summary of the entire execution process and output FINISHED. Do not revisit, re-evaluate, or re-execute any subtask that has already been completed.

## Tool call budget
Your total number of allowed tool calls is strictly limited — only slightly more than the number of subtasks in the plan. This budget is intentionally tight: it is enough to execute every subtask once with occasional retries, but not enough to repeat any subtask repeatedly or restart the entire plan. Excessive retries will consume the budget and prevent later subtasks from being executed at all.

## When invoking a tool, you must provide:
- The subtask content from the plan, passed as faithfully and completely as possible. Do not paraphrase, shorten, or omit details from the original subtask description. You may append clarifications, but never replace or reduce the original subtask content.
- All prior output and user-provided information that this subtask depends on, copied verbatim. No summaries. No references. The full actual text.

## Execution rules
- Execute subtasks in order, one at a time. Parallel tool calls are not allowed.
- Each subtask has a maximum of 3 attempts. Retrying is not required — only retry if you judge the result to be a clear failure or clearly insufficient. If the first attempt succeeds, move on immediately.
- If a subtask has been attempted 3 times and still fails, immediately write a detailed summary of the entire execution process so far — including what was attempted, what failed, and why it failed — then output FINISHED. Do not proceed to any remaining subtasks.
- Once all subtasks have been processed (either completed or exhausted their 3 attempts): write a detailed summary of every subtask's execution and result, then output FINISHED. Do this immediately — do not loop back, do not re-check, do not restart.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

function.name: PostgresManager

function.name: DocumentAnalyzer

function.name: MediaAnalyzer
function.description: A multimedia analysis agent capable of handling local images, audio, and video. It provides OCR extraction, AI-based visual understanding, metadata inspection, audio transcription and trimming, video analysis and summarization, and key-frame extraction. Supports common formats across images (JPG/PNG/GIF/TIFF/WEBP …), audio (MP3/WAV/FLAC/AAC/OGG …), and video (MP4/AVI/MOV/MKV/WEBM …). GIF and video content are processed as multi-frame sequences—similar to video key-frame extraction—while static image formats are analyzed as single frames. Designed to perform assigned multimedia tasks efficiently and return clear, structured results.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

function.name: PostgresManager
function.description: A database management agent responsible for inspecting, querying, and analyzing a PostgreSQL database. It can enumerate schemas and database objects, retrieve detailed metadata about tables and other objects, and execute SQL queries (with read-only restrictions when applicable). In addition, it supports query planning and performance analysis, including explaining query execution plans, identifying slow or resource-intensive queries, recommending indexes based on workloads or specific queries, and performing comprehensive database health checks covering caches, indexes, constraints, connections, and maintenance status.

          - paragraph [ref=e211]:
            - text: The 1977
            - link "New York Yankees" [ref=e212] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/New_York_Yankees
            - text: season was the 75th season for the Yankees. The team finished with a record of 100–62 and won the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e213] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: . The series victory was the 21st title in franchise history and the first under the ownership of
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e214] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: . New York was managed by
            - link "Billy Martin" [ref=e215] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Billy_Martin
            - text: and played at
            - link "Yankee Stadium" [ref=e216] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yankee_Stadium_(1923)
            - text: in
            - link "The Bronx" [ref=e217] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_Bronx
            - text: . The season was brought to life years later in the book and drama-documentary
            - generic [ref=e218]:
              - link "The Bronx is Burning" [ref=e219] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/The_Bronx_is_Burning
              - text: .
            - text: The Yankees also hosted the
            - link "1977 Major League Baseball All-Star Game" [ref=e220] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game
            - text: . To date, this is the most recent time the All-Star Game host team has won the World Series the same year.
          - generic [ref=e221]:
            - heading "Offseason" [level=2] [ref=e222]
            - generic [ref=e223]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e224] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=1
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e225]:
            - text: The Yankees signed
            - link "Reggie Jackson" [ref=e226] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Reggie_Jackson
            - text: to a five-year contract, totaling
            - link "$" [ref=e227] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/United_States_dollar
            - text: 2.96 million, on November 29, 1976. Upon arriving in New York, Jackson asked for uniform number 9, which he had worn in
            - link "Oakland" [ref=e228] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: and
            - link "Baltimore" [ref=e229] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1976_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: . However, that number was being worn by
            - link "third baseman" [ref=e230] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Third_baseman
            - link "Graig Nettles" [ref=e231] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Graig_Nettles
            - text: . So, noting that then-all-time home run leader
            - link "Hank Aaron" [ref=e232] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Hank_Aaron
            - text: had just retired, Jackson asked for and received number 44, Aaron's number.

          - paragraph [ref=e273]:
            - text: The team finished in first place in the
            - link "American League East" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_League_East
            - text: with a record of 100–62 (.617), 2½ games ahead of the
            - link "Baltimore Orioles" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: to successfully defend their division title. In the best-of-five
            - link "League Championship Series" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: (ALCS), they beat the
            - link "Kansas City Royals" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Kansas_City_Royals_season
            - text: in five games. In the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: ", New York defeated the"
            - link "Los Angeles Dodgers" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season
            - text: in six games.

            - heading "Reggie Jackson" [level=4] [ref=e832]
            - generic [ref=e833]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e834] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e835]:
            - text: Jackson's first season with the Yankees was a difficult one. Although team owner
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e836] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: and several players, most notably catcher and team captain
            - link "Thurman Munson" [ref=e837] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thurman_Munson
            - text: and outfielder
            - link "Lou Piniella" [ref=e838] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lou_Piniella
            - text: ", were excited about his arrival, Martin was not. He had managed the Detroit Tigers in"
            - link "1972" [ref=e839] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Detroit_Tigers_season
            - text: when Jackson's
            - link "A's" [ref=e840] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: beat them in the
            - link "league playoffs" [ref=e841] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: . Jackson was once quoted as saying of Martin, "I hate him, but if I played for him, I'd probably love him."
          - paragraph [ref=e842]:
            - text: The relationship between Jackson and his new teammates was strained due to an interview with
            - link "SPORT magazine" [ref=e843] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sport_(US_magazine)
            - text: writer
            - link "Robert Ward" [ref=e844] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Robert_Ward_(sportswriter)&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: . During
            - link "spring training" [ref=e845] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Spring_training
            - text: at the Yankees' camp in
            - link "Fort Lauderdale, Florida" [ref=e846] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida
            - text: ", Jackson and Ward were having drinks at a nearby bar. Jackson's version of the story is that he noted that the Yankees had won the pennant the year before, but lost the World Series to the Reds, and suggested that they needed one thing more to win it all, and pointed out the various ingredients in his drink. Ward suggested that Jackson might be \"the straw that stirs the drink.\" But when the story appeared in the May 1977 issue of SPORT, Ward quoted Jackson as saying, \"This team, it all flows from me. I'm the straw that stirs the drink. Maybe I should say me and Munson, but he can only stir it bad.\""
          - generic [ref=e847]:
            - heading "Thurman Munson" [level=4] [ref=e848]
            - generic [ref=e849]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e850] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e851]:
            - text: Thurman Munson was "uncharacteristically happy" about the team getting Jackson in large part because he believed he had received "a verbal agreement from Steinbrenner that, with the exception of Catfish Hunter (who'd signed a five-year, $3.75 million contract with the Yankees before the
            - link "1975" [ref=e852] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_New_York_Yankees_season
            - text: "season), he [Munson] would always be the highest-paid player on the team.\" But, Steinbrenner did not follow through and adjust Munson's contract upward. As the baseball book Stars and Strikes: Baseball and America in the Bicentennial Summer of ‘76 puts it, \"But the Yankee captain wouldn't be smiling for long, once he realized that Steinbrenner had no intention of making good on their agreement.\""
            - superscript [ref=e853]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e854] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stars_and_Strikes,_pages_365-66-12"
          - paragraph [ref=e855]:
            - text: An article in
            - link "The New York Times" [ref=e857] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_New_York_Times
            - text: in January 1977 reported, "Munson, however, has continued to be disturbed with Steinbrenner because of what he said first was the owner's denial of any verbal agreement and secand [second] was Steinbrenner's misleading him on Jackson's salary."
            - superscript [ref=e858]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e859] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
          - generic [ref=e860]:
            - heading "Billy Martin" [level=4] [ref=e861]
            - generic [ref=e862]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e863] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=13
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e864]:
            - text: Martin feuded publicly with both Yankee owner Steinbrenner and star outfielder Jackson. In one especially infamous incident on Saturday, June 18, in the second game of a three-game sweep by the
            - link "Boston Red Sox" [ref=e865] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Boston_Red_Sox_season
            - text: at
            - link "Fenway Park" [ref=e866] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fenway_Park
            - text: ", Martin pulled Jackson off the field in mid-inning for failing to hustle on a check-swing pop double by Boston's"
            - link "Jim Rice" [ref=e867] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jim_Rice
            - text: . Replaced in right field by Paul Blair, Jackson confronted Martin when he returned to the dugout, and Martin had to be restrained by his coaches (
            - link "Elston Howard" [ref=e868] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Elston_Howard
            - text: and
            - link "Yogi Berra" [ref=e869] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yogi_Berra
            - text: ) from fighting with Jackson during the nationally televised
            - link "Game of the Week" [ref=e871] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Major_League_Baseball_Game_of_the_Week
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e872]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-ppclsh-14"

            - text: about the turmoil in New York City in 1977, including the

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - heading "Reggie Jackson" [level=4] [ref=e832]
            - generic [ref=e833]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e834] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e835]:
            - text: Jackson's first season with the Yankees was a difficult one. Although team owner
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e836] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: and several players, most notably catcher and team captain
            - link "Thurman Munson" [ref=e837] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thurman_Munson
            - text: and outfielder
            - link "Lou Piniella" [ref=e838] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lou_Piniella
            - text: ", were excited about his arrival, Martin was not. He had managed the Detroit Tigers in"
            - link "1972" [ref=e839] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Detroit_Tigers_season
            - text: when Jackson's
            - link "A's" [ref=e840] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: beat them in the
            - link "league playoffs" [ref=e841] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: . Jackson was once quoted as saying of Martin, "I hate him, but if I played for him, I'd probably love him."
          - paragraph [ref=e842]:
            - text: The relationship between Jackson and his new teammates was strained due to an interview with
            - link "SPORT magazine" [ref=e843] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sport_(US_magazine)
            - text: writer
            - link "Robert Ward" [ref=e844] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Robert_Ward_(sportswriter)&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: . During
            - link "spring training" [ref=e845] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Spring_training
            - text: at the Yankees' camp in
            - link "Fort Lauderdale, Florida" [ref=e846] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida
            - text: ", Jackson and Ward were having drinks at a nearby bar. Jackson's version of the story is that he noted that the Yankees had won the pennant the year before, but lost the World Series to the Reds, and suggested that they needed one thing more to win it all, and pointed out the various ingredients in his drink. Ward suggested that Jackson might be \"the straw that stirs the drink.\" But when the story appeared in the May 1977 issue of SPORT, Ward quoted Jackson as saying, \"This team, it all flows from me. I'm the straw that stirs the drink. Maybe I should say me and Munson, but he can only stir it bad.\""
          - generic [ref=e847]:
            - heading "Thurman Munson" [level=4] [ref=e848]
            - generic [ref=e849]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e850] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e851]:
            - text: Thurman Munson was "uncharacteristically happy" about the team getting Jackson in large part because he believed he had received "a verbal agreement from Steinbrenner that, with the exception of Catfish Hunter (who'd signed a five-year, $3.75 million contract with the Yankees before the
            - link "1975" [ref=e852] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_New_York_Yankees_season
            - text: "season), he [Munson] would always be the highest-paid player on the team.\" But, Steinbrenner did not follow through and adjust Munson's contract upward. As the baseball book Stars and Strikes: Baseball and America in the Bicentennial Summer of ‘76 puts it, \"But the Yankee captain wouldn't be smiling for long, once he realized that Steinbrenner had no intention of making good on their agreement.\""
            - superscript [ref=e853]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e854] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stars_and_Strikes,_pages_365-66-12"
          - paragraph [ref=e855]:
            - text: An article in
            - link "The New York Times" [ref=e857] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_New_York_Times
            - text: in January 1977 reported, "Munson, however, has continued to be disturbed with Steinbrenner because of what he said first was the owner's denial of any verbal agreement and secand [second] was Steinbrenner's misleading him on Jackson's salary."
            - superscript [ref=e858]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e859] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
          - generic [ref=e860]:
            - heading "Billy Martin" [level=4] [ref=e861]
            - generic [ref=e862]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e863] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=13
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e864]:
            - text: Martin feuded publicly with both Yankee owner Steinbrenner and star outfielder Jackson. In one especially infamous incident on Saturday, June 18, in the second game of a three-game sweep by the
            - link "Boston Red Sox" [ref=e865] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Boston_Red_Sox_season
            - text: at
            - link "Fenway Park" [ref=e866] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fenway_Park
            - text: ", Martin pulled Jackson off the field in mid-inning for failing to hustle on a check-swing pop double by Boston's"
            - link "Jim Rice" [ref=e867] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jim_Rice
            - text: . Replaced in right field by Paul Blair, Jackson confronted Martin when he returned to the dugout, and Martin had to be restrained by his coaches (
            - link "Elston Howard" [ref=e868] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Elston_Howard
            - text: and
            - link "Yogi Berra" [ref=e869] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yogi_Berra
            - text: ) from fighting with Jackson during the nationally televised
            - link "Game of the Week" [ref=e871] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Major_League_Baseball_Game_of_the_Week
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e872]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-ppclsh-14"
            - superscript [ref=e874]:

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

          - paragraph [ref=e273]:
            - text: The team finished in first place in the
            - link "American League East" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_League_East
            - text: with a record of 100–62 (.617), 2½ games ahead of the
            - link "Baltimore Orioles" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: to successfully defend their division title. In the best-of-five
            - link "League Championship Series" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: (ALCS), they beat the
            - link "Kansas City Royals" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Kansas_City_Royals_season
            - text: in five games. In the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: ", New York defeated the"
            - link "Los Angeles Dodgers" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season
            - text: in six games.

          - generic [ref=e831]:
            - heading "Reggie Jackson" [level=4] [ref=e832]
            - generic [ref=e833]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e834] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e835]:
            - text: Jackson's first season with the Yankees was a difficult one. Although team owner
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e836] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: and several players, most notably catcher and team captain
            - link "Thurman Munson" [ref=e837] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thurman_Munson
            - text: and outfielder
            - link "Lou Piniella" [ref=e838] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lou_Piniella
            - text: ", were excited about his arrival, Martin was not. He had managed the Detroit Tigers in"
            - link "1972" [ref=e839] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Detroit_Tigers_season
            - text: when Jackson's
            - link "A's" [ref=e840] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: beat them in the
            - link "league playoffs" [ref=e841] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: . Jackson was once quoted as saying of Martin, "I hate him, but if I played for him, I'd probably love him."
          - paragraph [ref=e842]:
            - text: The relationship between Jackson and his new teammates was strained due to an interview with
            - link "SPORT magazine" [ref=e843] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sport_(US_magazine)
            - text: writer
            - link "Robert Ward" [ref=e844] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Robert_Ward_(sportswriter)&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: . During
            - link "spring training" [ref=e845] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Spring_training
            - text: at the Yankees' camp in
            - link "Fort Lauderdale, Florida" [ref=e846] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida
            - text: ", Jackson and Ward were having drinks at a nearby bar. Jackson's version of the story is that he noted that the Yankees had won the pennant the year before, but lost the World Series to the Reds, and suggested that they needed one thing more to win it all, and pointed out the various ingredients in his drink. Ward suggested that Jackson might be \"the straw that stirs the drink.\" But when the story appeared in the May 1977 issue of SPORT, Ward quoted Jackson as saying, \"This team, it all flows from me. I'm the straw that stirs the drink. Maybe I should say me and Munson, but he can only stir it bad.\""
          - generic [ref=e847]:
            - heading "Thurman Munson" [level=4] [ref=e848]
            - generic [ref=e849]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e850] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e851]:
            - text: Thurman Munson was "uncharacteristically happy" about the team getting Jackson in large part because he believed he had received "a verbal agreement from Steinbrenner that, with the exception of Catfish Hunter (who'd signed a five-year, $3.75 million contract with the Yankees before the
            - link "1975" [ref=e852] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_New_York_Yankees_season
            - text: "season), he [Munson] would always be the highest-paid player on the team.\" But, Steinbrenner did not follow through and adjust Munson's contract upward. As the baseball book Stars and Strikes: Baseball and America in the Bicentennial Summer of ‘76 puts it, \"But the Yankee captain wouldn't be smiling for long, once he realized that Steinbrenner had no intention of making good on their agreement.\""
            - superscript [ref=e853]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e854] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stars_and_Strikes,_pages_365-66-12"
          - paragraph [ref=e855]:
            - text: An article in
            - link "The New York Times" [ref=e857] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_New_York_Times
            - text: in January 1977 reported, "Munson, however, has continued to be disturbed with Steinbrenner because of what he said first was the owner's denial of any verbal agreement and secand [second] was Steinbrenner's misleading him on Jackson's salary."
            - superscript [ref=e858]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e859] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
          - generic [ref=e860]:
            - heading "Billy Martin" [level=4] [ref=e861]
            - generic [ref=e862]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e863] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=13
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e864]:
            - text: Martin feuded publicly with both Yankee owner Steinbrenner and star outfielder Jackson. In one especially infamous incident on Saturday, June 18, in the second game of a three-game sweep by the
            - link "Boston Red Sox" [ref=e865] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Boston_Red_Sox_season
            - text: at
            - link "Fenway Park" [ref=e866] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fenway_Park
            - text: ", Martin pulled Jackson off the field in mid-inning for failing to hustle on a check-swing pop double by Boston's"
            - link "Jim Rice" [ref=e867] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jim_Rice
            - text: . Replaced in right field by Paul Blair, Jackson confronted Martin when he returned to the dugout, and Martin had to be restrained by his coaches (
            - link "Elston Howard" [ref=e868] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Elston_Howard
            - text: and
            - link "Yogi Berra" [ref=e869] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yogi_Berra
            - text: ) from fighting with Jackson during the nationally televised
            - link "Game of the Week" [ref=e871] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Major_League_Baseball_Game_of_the_Week
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e872]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e873] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ppclsh-14"
            - superscript [ref=e874]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-ergftsj-15"
            - superscript [ref=e876]:

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e225]:
            - text: The Yankees signed
            - link "Reggie Jackson" [ref=e226] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Reggie_Jackson
            - text: to a five-year contract, totaling
            - link "$" [ref=e227] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/United_States_dollar
            - text: 2.96 million, on November 29, 1976. Upon arriving in New York, Jackson asked for uniform number 9, which he had worn in
            - link "Oakland" [ref=e228] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: and
            - link "Baltimore" [ref=e229] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1976_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: . However, that number was being worn by
            - link "third baseman" [ref=e230] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Third_baseman
            - link "Graig Nettles" [ref=e231] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Graig_Nettles
            - text: . So, noting that then-all-time home run leader
            - link "Hank Aaron" [ref=e232] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Hank_Aaron
            - text: had just retired, Jackson asked for and received number 44, Aaron's number.

              - link "Rick Bladt" [ref=e251] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "Baltimore Orioles" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "Texas Rangers" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e273]:
            - text: The team finished in first place in the
            - link "American League East" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_League_East
            - text: with a record of 100–62 (.617), 2½ games ahead of the
            - link "Baltimore Orioles" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: to successfully defend their division title. In the best-of-five
            - link "League Championship Series" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: (ALCS), they beat the
            - link "Kansas City Royals" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Kansas_City_Royals_season
            - text: in five games. In the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: ", New York defeated the"
            - link "Los Angeles Dodgers" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season
            - text: in six games.

            - text: Yankee Stadium hosted the

            - text: on July 19, less than a week after the

            - link "Reggie Jackson" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and third baseman
            - link "Graig Nettles" [ref=e711] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "National League" [ref=e712] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: defeated the American League 7–5.

            - generic [ref=e833]:
              - text: "["

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e835]:
            - text: Jackson's first season with the Yankees was a difficult one. Although team owner
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e836] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: and several players, most notably catcher and team captain
            - link "Thurman Munson" [ref=e837] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thurman_Munson
            - text: and outfielder
            - link "Lou Piniella" [ref=e838] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lou_Piniella
            - text: ", were excited about his arrival, Martin was not. He had managed the Detroit Tigers in"
            - link "1972" [ref=e839] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Detroit_Tigers_season
            - text: when Jackson's
            - link "A's" [ref=e840] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: beat them in the
            - link "league playoffs" [ref=e841] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: . Jackson was once quoted as saying of Martin, "I hate him, but if I played for him, I'd probably love him."
          - paragraph [ref=e842]:
            - text: The relationship between Jackson and his new teammates was strained due to an interview with
            - link "SPORT magazine" [ref=e843] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sport_(US_magazine)
            - text: writer
            - link "Robert Ward" [ref=e844] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Robert_Ward_(sportswriter)&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: . During
            - link "spring training" [ref=e845] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Spring_training
            - text: at the Yankees' camp in
            - link "Fort Lauderdale, Florida" [ref=e846] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida
            - text: ", Jackson and Ward were having drinks at a nearby bar. Jackson's version of the story is that he noted that the Yankees had won the pennant the year before, but lost the World Series to the Reds, and suggested that they needed one thing more to win it all, and pointed out the various ingredients in his drink. Ward suggested that Jackson might be \"the straw that stirs the drink.\" But when the story appeared in the May 1977 issue of SPORT, Ward quoted Jackson as saying, \"This team, it all flows from me. I'm the straw that stirs the drink. Maybe I should say me and Munson, but he can only stir it bad.\""
          - generic [ref=e847]:
            - heading "Thurman Munson" [level=4] [ref=e848]
            - generic [ref=e849]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e850] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e851]:
            - text: Thurman Munson was "uncharacteristically happy" about the team getting Jackson in large part because he believed he had received "a verbal agreement from Steinbrenner that, with the exception of Catfish Hunter (who'd signed a five-year, $3.75 million contract with the Yankees before the
            - link "1975" [ref=e852] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_New_York_Yankees_season
            - text: "season), he [Munson] would always be the highest-paid player on the team.\" But, Steinbrenner did not follow through and adjust Munson's contract upward. As the baseball book Stars and Strikes: Baseball and America in the Bicentennial Summer of ‘76 puts it, \"But the Yankee captain wouldn't be smiling for long, once he realized that Steinbrenner had no intention of making good on their agreement.\""
            - superscript [ref=e853]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e854] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stars_and_Strikes,_pages_365-66-12"
          - paragraph [ref=e855]:
            - text: An article in
            - link "The New York Times" [ref=e857] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_New_York_Times
            - text: in January 1977 reported, "Munson, however, has continued to be disturbed with Steinbrenner because of what he said first was the owner's denial of any verbal agreement and secand [second] was Steinbrenner's misleading him on Jackson's salary."
            - superscript [ref=e858]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e859] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
          - generic [ref=e860]:
            - heading "Billy Martin" [level=4] [ref=e861]

              - text: "["

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e864]:
            - text: Martin feuded publicly with both Yankee owner Steinbrenner and star outfielder Jackson. In one especially infamous incident on Saturday, June 18, in the second game of a three-game sweep by the
            - link "Boston Red Sox" [ref=e865] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Boston_Red_Sox_season
            - text: at
            - link "Fenway Park" [ref=e866] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fenway_Park
            - text: ", Martin pulled Jackson off the field in mid-inning for failing to hustle on a check-swing pop double by Boston's"
            - link "Jim Rice" [ref=e867] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jim_Rice
            - text: . Replaced in right field by Paul Blair, Jackson confronted Martin when he returned to the dugout, and Martin had to be restrained by his coaches (
            - link "Elston Howard" [ref=e868] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Elston_Howard
            - text: and
            - link "Yogi Berra" [ref=e869] [cursor=pointer]:

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e292]:
            - text: The 1977
            - link "New York Yankees" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/New_York_Yankees
            - text: season was the 75th season for the Yankees. The team finished with a record of 100–62 and won the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e294] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: . The series victory was the 21st title in franchise history and the first under the ownership of
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: . New York was managed by
            - link "Billy Martin" [ref=e296] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Billy_Martin
            - text: and played at
            - link "Yankee Stadium" [ref=e297] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yankee_Stadium_(1923)
            - text: in
            - link "The Bronx" [ref=e298] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_Bronx
            - text: . The season was brought to life years later in the book and drama-documentary
            - generic [ref=e299]:
              - link "The Bronx is Burning" [ref=e300] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/The_Bronx_is_Burning
              - text: .
            - text: The Yankees also hosted the
            - link "1977 Major League Baseball All-Star Game" [ref=e301] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game
            - text: . To date, this is the most recent time the All-Star Game host team has won the World Series the same year.
          - generic [ref=e302]:
            - heading "Offseason" [level=2] [ref=e303]
            - generic [ref=e304]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e305] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=1
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e306]:
            - text: The Yankees signed
            - link "Reggie Jackson" [ref=e307] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Reggie_Jackson
            - text: to a five-year contract, totaling
            - link "$" [ref=e308] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/United_States_dollar
            - text: 2.96 million, on November 29, 1976. Upon arriving in New York, Jackson asked for uniform number 9, which he had worn in
            - link "Oakland" [ref=e309] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: and
            - link "Baltimore" [ref=e310] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1976_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: . However, that number was being worn by
            - link "third baseman" [ref=e311] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Third_baseman
            - link "Graig Nettles" [ref=e312] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Graig_Nettles
            - text: . So, noting that then-all-time home run leader
            - link "Hank Aaron" [ref=e313] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Hank_Aaron
            - text: had just retired, Jackson asked for and received number 44, Aaron's number.

          - paragraph [ref=e354]:
            - text: The team finished in first place in the
            - link "American League East" [ref=e355] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_League_East
            - text: with a record of 100–62 (.617), 2½ games ahead of the
            - link "Baltimore Orioles" [ref=e356] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Baltimore_Orioles_season
            - text: to successfully defend their division title. In the best-of-five
            - link "League Championship Series" [ref=e357] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: (ALCS), they beat the
            - link "Kansas City Royals" [ref=e358] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Kansas_City_Royals_season
            - text: in five games. In the
            - link "World Series" [ref=e359] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_World_Series
            - text: ", New York defeated the"
            - link "Los Angeles Dodgers" [ref=e360] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Los_Angeles_Dodgers_season
            - text: in six games.

            - heading "Reggie Jackson" [level=4] [ref=e913]
            - generic [ref=e914]:
              - text: "["

          - paragraph [ref=e916]:
            - text: Jackson's first season with the Yankees was a difficult one. Although team owner
            - link "George Steinbrenner" [ref=e917] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Steinbrenner
            - text: and several players, most notably catcher and team captain
            - link "Thurman Munson" [ref=e918] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thurman_Munson
            - text: and outfielder
            - link "Lou Piniella" [ref=e919] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lou_Piniella
            - text: ", were excited about his arrival, Martin was not. He had managed the Detroit Tigers in"
            - link "1972" [ref=e920] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Detroit_Tigers_season
            - text: when Jackson's
            - link "A's" [ref=e921] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_Oakland_Athletics_season
            - text: beat them in the
            - link "league playoffs" [ref=e922] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1972_American_League_Championship_Series
            - text: . Jackson was once quoted as saying of Martin, "I hate him, but if I played for him, I'd probably love him."
          - paragraph [ref=e923]:
            - text: The relationship between Jackson and his new teammates was strained due to an interview with
            - link "SPORT magazine" [ref=e924] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sport_(US_magazine)
            - text: writer
            - link "Robert Ward" [ref=e925] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Robert_Ward_(sportswriter)&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: . During
            - link "spring training" [ref=e926] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Spring_training
            - text: at the Yankees' camp in
            - link "Fort Lauderdale, Florida" [ref=e927] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fort_Lauderdale,_Florida
            - text: ", Jackson and Ward were having drinks at a nearby bar. Jackson's version of the story is that he noted that the Yankees had won the pennant the year before, but lost the World Series to the Reds, and suggested that they needed one thing more to win it all, and pointed out the various ingredients in his drink. Ward suggested that Jackson might be \"the straw that stirs the drink.\" But when the story appeared in the May 1977 issue of SPORT, Ward quoted Jackson as saying, \"This team, it all flows from me. I'm the straw that stirs the drink. Maybe I should say me and Munson, but he can only stir it bad.\""
          - generic [ref=e928]:
            - heading "Thurman Munson" [level=4] [ref=e929]
            - generic [ref=e930]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e931] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e932]:
            - text: Thurman Munson was "uncharacteristically happy" about the team getting Jackson in large part because he believed he had received "a verbal agreement from Steinbrenner that, with the exception of Catfish Hunter (who'd signed a five-year, $3.75 million contract with the Yankees before the
            - link "1975" [ref=e933] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1975_New_York_Yankees_season
            - text: "season), he [Munson] would always be the highest-paid player on the team.\" But, Steinbrenner did not follow through and adjust Munson's contract upward. As the baseball book Stars and Strikes: Baseball and America in the Bicentennial Summer of ‘76 puts it, \"But the Yankee captain wouldn't be smiling for long, once he realized that Steinbrenner had no intention of making good on their agreement.\""
            - superscript [ref=e934]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e935] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stars_and_Strikes,_pages_365-66-12"
          - paragraph [ref=e936]:
            - text: An article in
            - link "The New York Times" [ref=e938] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/The_New_York_Times
            - text: in January 1977 reported, "Munson, however, has continued to be disturbed with Steinbrenner because of what he said first was the owner's denial of any verbal agreement and secand [second] was Steinbrenner's misleading him on Jackson's salary."
            - superscript [ref=e939]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e940] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
          - generic [ref=e941]:
            - heading "Billy Martin" [level=4] [ref=e942]
            - generic [ref=e943]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e944] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=1977_New_York_Yankees_season&action=edit&section=13
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e945]:
            - text: Martin feuded publicly with both Yankee owner Steinbrenner and star outfielder Jackson. In one especially infamous incident on Saturday, June 18, in the second game of a three-game sweep by the
            - link "Boston Red Sox" [ref=e946] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1977_Boston_Red_Sox_season
            - text: at
            - link "Fenway Park" [ref=e947] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fenway_Park
            - text: ", Martin pulled Jackson off the field in mid-inning for failing to hustle on a check-swing pop double by Boston's"
            - link "Jim Rice" [ref=e948] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jim_Rice
            - text: . Replaced in right field by Paul Blair, Jackson confronted Martin when he returned to the dugout, and Martin had to be restrained by his coaches (
            - link "Elston Howard" [ref=e949] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Elston_Howard
            - text: and
            - link "Yogi Berra" [ref=e950] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Yogi_Berra
            - text: ) from fighting with Jackson during the nationally televised
            - link "Game of the Week" [ref=e952] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Major_League_Baseball_Game_of_the_Week
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e953]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-ppclsh-14"

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.
